1.pericope_label: O Lord God of my salvation, I have cried day and night before thee

schools.summary: Delitzsch places the psalm rather than explaining it: set beside the cheerful psalm before it as a contrast, it is the gloomiest of all the plaintive psalms — not Psalm 77, which the old expositors used to name — and though the title 'God of my salvation' shows the spark of faith is not out, the gloom never rises into hope and the psalm dies away in Job-like lamentation.

Calvin turns the question of authorship into a question of use: God exercised Heman, whom he had adorned with such gifts, not for his servant's sake only but so that Heman might mount an elevated stage and testify his infirmities along with his faith to the whole Church, the psalm serving as a form of prayer for the afflicted on the brink of despair; and he reads the brief opening as a bridle laid on the poet's own feelings. Gill hears in the title both temporal and spiritual salvation, and a faith never so low that the Lord could not still be called his own.

Clarke assembles everything that has been said about the title — his own responsive rendering, Kennicott's leper shut up in a separate house, Calmet's captivity, the genealogy that would make these the oldest poems extant — and then throws the whole enquiry over, holding that to labour at reconciling the psalm titles is to treat them with too much respect, since many are wrongly placed and none are inspired.

Henry and Spurgeon agree that the first words are the only light in the psalm. Henry notes that Heman, a seer and a comforter of others, could see no comfort for himself and had nothing about him but clouds and darkness; Spurgeon answers that while a man can see God as his Saviour it is not altogether midnight, and reads the crying day and night as a prayer that distress had quickened rather than extinguished.

Augustine reads the title as the psalm's subject, rendering its unique phrase 'for the chorus' and hearing in it the Passion — Christ going before as precentor with the choir of martyrs taking up the strain, the sons of Korah being the imitators of that Passion — but warning that since the choir signifies a concord that consists in charity, a man may give his body to be burnt and still not answer in it.

debates.question: How much weight should the title carry?

positions.summary: Almost none: labouring to reconcile the matters contained in the psalm titles treats them with too much respect, since many are wrongly placed and none of them are divinely inspired.
It is the subject of the psalm: the phrase found nowhere else means 'for the chorus', and the responding is the choir of martyrs taking up the strain after Christ their precentor.
The name it gives God — God of my salvation — is the one thing in the psalm that is not dark, and is the only ray of comfortable light in it.
Leprosy, on Kennicott's view: the prayer of a man shut up in a separate house in the last stage of the disease, which under the Mosaic dispensation was taken to come from the immediate stroke of God.
The captivity, on Calmet's view, the nation figured as one man afflicted through the whole course of his life; or, on Kimchi's, a captive speaking as a slave under his chains.
The particular affliction does not matter: what matters is that a man so eminently gifted was so overwhelmed, since that is what makes the psalm usable by everyone on the brink of despair.

outliers.summary: Observes that most men complain under grief but few pour their groanings out before God — the majority court retirement in order to murmur against him, while others cry into the air at random — so that it is a rare virtue to set God before our eyes at all.

Notes that had Heman's pain not been incessant his supplications might have been intermittent, and concludes that it is a good thing sickness will not let us rest if we spend the restlessness in prayer.

themes: O Lord God of my salvation, I have cried day and night before thee:

2.pericope_label: Let my prayer come before thee: incline thine ear unto my cry... Lord, I have called daily upon thee, I have stretched out my hands unto thee

schools.summary: Ellicott supplies the argument that holds the section together — Sheol severs the covenant relation with God, which is the irresistible reason why the prayer must be heard now — and works the Hebrew verse by verse: a hero whose strength is gone, pressed down with all thy breakers, a figurative rather than an actual shutting up, an eye that fades or pines. On 'free among the dead' he sets out the whole history of the word and decides for the sense of the Latin defunctus. Delitzsch hears Job behind the complaint about alienated relations, and marks verse 9 as the point where the sufferer gathers himself up afresh for prayer.

Gill keeps the temple and the Passion in view: the prayer is not to be shut out but to ascend perfumed with the much incense of the mediation, the soul is glutted with troubles as a stomach with meat, and the man counted with those who go down to the pit is Christ numbered with transgressors and crucified between two.

Clarke reads the section through images and antiquities: the Homeric allegory of Prayers as the lame daughters of Jove limping after swift-footed Offence, the field of battle where spoilers strip the dead and the mortally wounded alike, the army roll from which the killed are erased into a black book, and the tempest at sea whose waves cover the ship. Wesley glosses briefly and plainly — discharged from the warfare of this life, afflicted with judgments that break in like waves.

debates.question: What does 'free among the dead' mean?

positions.summary: Free in the sense of the Latin defunctus — done with, discharged. The old versions without exception take the word as an adjective, as of an emancipated slave or of freedom from public burdens, and the Targum explains it as freed from legal duties.
Not free but stripped: verses 4 and 5 describe a field of battle where the spoilers go among the fallen and strip the dead and the mortally wounded who are too feeble to resist.
Well nigh discharged from the warfare of this life and entered as a member into the society of the dead — a man as neglected as a corpse.
Gesenius makes the word a noun instead, and renders the clause 'among the dead is my couch'.

debates.question: Is the shutting up of verse 8 literal?

positions.summary: It describes a leper, abominable to all because of the infectious nature of the disease and at last shut up in a separate house.
Not necessarily an actual imprisonment or incarceration, but another figurative way of describing great trouble, with a page of Job before the poet.

outliers.summary: Notes that 'cut off from thy hand' suggests the roll in which a general enters his whole army, the killed being erased and written into a separate book of death as against the book of life — and observes drily that from this circumstance the doctrine of unconditional reprobation and election has been derived.
Marks that the sufferer's complaints are themselves petitions, precisely because they are complaints poured out before God rather than anywhere else.

themes: Let my prayer come before thee: incline thine ear unto my cry;
For my soul is full of troubles: and my life draweth nigh unto the grave.
I am counted with them that go down into the pit: I am as a man that hath no strength:
Free among the dead, like the slain that lie in the grave, whom thou rememberest no more: and they are cut off from thy hand.
Thou hast laid me in the lowest pit, in darkness, in the deeps.
Thy wrath lieth hard upon me, and thou hast afflicted me with all thy waves. Selah.
Thou hast put away mine acquaintance far from me; thou hast made me an abomination unto them: I am shut up, and I cannot come forth.
Mine eye mourneth by reason of affliction: Lord, I have called daily upon thee, I have stretched out my hands unto thee.

10.pericope_label: Wilt thou shew wonders to the dead? shall the dead arise and praise thee?... Lover and friend hast thou put far from me, and mine acquaintance into darkness

schools.summary: Ellicott holds that the four questions are not about resurrection as we understand it, since that hope had hardly dawned on Israel: the underworld is one vast sepulchre of languid shapes cut off from the upper air but conscious of the monotony of death, and lovingkindness, faithfulness, wonders and righteousness are all covenant words which the grave knew nothing of. He makes the pronoun of verse 13 emphatic, finds loathing in the verb of verse 14, puzzles at a word for 'distracted' that occurs nowhere else, and corrects the last clause to 'darkness is my friend'.

Gill answers the questions in the affirmative from the other side of the resurrection: God does show wonders to the dead in trespasses by quickening them, and showed them to Christ before he saw corruption; and he hears in the last verse the disciples who forsook Christ.

Clarke reads the interrogations as the strongest possible negations and draws doctrine from the second of them — faithfulness covers God's threatenings as well as his promises, but annihilation is no punishment — then illustrates the land of forgetfulness from the heathen river Lethe and closes the psalm with a Persian poet whose echo answers his question about the dead with the question itself. Wesley states the plain sense: the grave, where men are forgotten by their nearest relations.

Henry refuses to hear despair in the expostulation or any denial of the last resurrection — it pleads for speedy relief, since deceased bodies can neither receive God's favours in comfort nor return them in praise — and reads the rest pastorally: God prevents our prayers with his mercies and we should prevent his mercies with our prayers; nothing grieves a child of God like the hidden face; even those designed for God's favours may for a time suffer his terrors; and to be friendless is almost to be comfortless.

debates.question: What do the questions about the dead assume?

positions.summary: A Hebrew conception of the underworld in which the dead lie silent and motionless, oblivious of the upper air; the hope of a final resurrection had hardly yet dawned, and the questions are not about it.
Nothing against the resurrection at the last day; the expostulation is a plea for speedy relief, since deceased bodies can neither receive God's favours in comfort nor return them in praise.
They can be answered yes: God shows wonders to the dead in trespasses by quickening them, and showed them to Christ before he saw corruption.

debates.question: How should the last clause of the psalm be rendered?

positions.summary: 'Mine acquaintance into darkness' is an erroneous rendering; read 'darkness is my friend', having taken the place of those who were removed.
Keep the received sense: lover and friend put far away is the aggravating circumstance that closes the psalm, and next to the comforts of religion are those of friendship.

outliers.summary: Argues from 'thy faithfulness in destruction' that God cannot intend to annihilate the wicked, since faithfulness covers his threatenings as much as his promises and annihilation would be no punishment at all.

themes: Wilt thou shew wonders to the dead? shall the dead arise and praise thee? Selah.
Shall thy lovingkindness be declared in the grave? or thy faithfulness in destruction?
Shall thy wonders be known in the dark? and thy righteousness in the land of forgetfulness?
But unto thee have I cried, O Lord; and in the morning shall my prayer prevent thee.
Lord, why castest thou off my soul? why hidest thou thy face from me?
I am afflicted and ready to die from my youth up: while I suffer thy terrors I am distracted.
Thy fierce wrath goeth over me; thy terrors have cut me off.
They came round about me daily like water; they compassed me about together.
Lover and friend hast thou put far from me, and mine acquaintance into darkness.
